## Decision

Panics reachable from a rayon `.map()`, a `DocgenPlugin` hook, or a NAPI entry point are caught at `crates/core/src/panic_guard.rs`'s `pub fn contain_panic<T>(label: &str, f: impl FnOnce() -> T) -> Result<T, Diagnostic>`, converting the payload into a `Diagnostic` tagged `DiagnosticCode::InternalPanic` instead of aborting a batch, killing the whole pipeline, or poisoning a lock. `contain_panic` wraps its closure in `AssertUnwindSafe` internally, so callers never reason about `UnwindSafe` themselves — this matters because the plugin-hook call sites pass `&mut SourceData`/`&mut ComponentEntry`, and `&mut T` is unconditionally `!UnwindSafe` in std. The internal `AssertUnwindSafe` is justified by this codebase's data shape: `SourceData` and `ComponentEntry` have no interior mutability (`Cell`/`RefCell`) that could leave a torn, observable half-write behind a caught panic — the whole per-item operation is what gets abandoned, not a partial mutation trusted afterward.

`contain_panic` wraps the rayon parse-phase and resolve-phase closure bodies in `pipeline/mod.rs`, each individual `plugin.on_x(...)` call inside `PluginRegistry::run_on_file_extracted`/`run_on_component_resolved` in `plugin.rs` (not the whole loop, so one bad plugin degrades only itself), and all five NAPI entry points in `crates/binding/src/lib.rs`. `watch.rs`'s poisoned-lock `.expect()` was also replaced with `.unwrap_or_else(|p| p.into_inner())` as defense in depth.

# 0005. Contain panics at a single, per-item boundary

**Status:** Accepted **Date:** 2026-08-05

## Context

There was no `catch_unwind` anywhere in the repo. Panic safety existed only by accident: `extract_all`, `extract_file_incremental`, and `initialize_session` happened to run inside `tokio::task::spawn_blocking`, whose `JoinError` catches an unwind as a side effect of tokio's own plumbing, not a decision anyone made. `pipeline/mod.rs`'s rayon `.map()` closures had no per-item boundary, `plugin.rs` called each `DocgenPlugin` hook with zero isolation between plugins, `create_session`/`close_session` skipped `spawn_blocking` entirely and got no protection at all, and `watch.rs`'s `std::sync::Mutex` could poison permanently as a direct consequence of an unprotected panic happening while the lock was held.

## Decision

Panics reachable from a rayon `.map()`, a `DocgenPlugin` hook, or a NAPI entry point are caught at `crates/core/src/panic_guard.rs`'s `pub fn contain_panic<T>(label: &str, f: impl FnOnce() -> T) -> Result<T, Diagnostic>`, converting the payload into a `Diagnostic` tagged `DiagnosticCode::InternalPanic` instead of aborting a batch, killing the whole pipeline, or poisoning a lock. `contain_panic` wraps its closure in `AssertUnwindSafe` internally, so callers never reason about `UnwindSafe` themselves — this matters because the plugin-hook call sites pass `&mut SourceData`/`&mut ComponentEntry`, and `&mut T` is unconditionally `!UnwindSafe` in std. The internal `AssertUnwindSafe` is justified by this codebase's data shape: `SourceData` and `ComponentEntry` have no interior mutability (`Cell`/`RefCell`) that could leave a torn, observable half-write behind a caught panic — the whole per-item operation is what gets abandoned, not a partial mutation trusted afterward.

`contain_panic` wraps the rayon parse-phase and resolve-phase closure bodies in `pipeline/mod.rs`, each individual `plugin.on_x(...)` call inside `PluginRegistry::run_on_file_extracted`/`run_on_component_resolved` in `plugin.rs` (not the whole loop, so one bad plugin degrades only itself), and all five NAPI entry points in `crates/binding/src/lib.rs`. `watch.rs`'s poisoned-lock `.expect()` was also replaced with `.unwrap_or_else(|p| p.into_inner())` as defense in depth.

## Consequences

- One bad file, plugin, or session call degrades to a diagnostic instead of taking down its batch, the pipeline, or the session.
- `PluginRegistry::run_on_file_extracted` and `run_on_component_resolved` changed their return type from `()` to `Vec<Diagnostic>` to carry caught-panic diagnostics back to the pipeline — a real API change, not just internal wiring.
- `extract_all`, `extract_file_incremental`, and `initialize_session` were already panic-safe via `spawn_blocking`'s `JoinError`; wrapping their bodies in `contain_panic` makes that guarantee documented and consistent with the rest of the codebase rather than incidental. `create_session` and `close_session` were genuinely unprotected before this and are now wrapped directly.
- `watch.rs`'s `std::sync::Mutex` poisoning is now defense-in-depth rather than a live risk — panics upstream (rayon batches, plugin hooks) are contained before they'd reach that lock while held.
- Every future concurrent, plugin, or FFI entry point has one obvious place to route through instead of re-deriving the answer.

## Alternatives considered

napi-rs (the pinned version) has its own opt-in `#[napi(catch_unwind)]` attribute that wraps a function body in `catch_unwind` at the FFI boundary. It would work for the five NAPI entry points, but we used `contain_panic` explicitly there too, for one mechanism across rayon, plugins, and FFI instead of two.

# Status

**Updated:** 2026-08-13

Core extraction, resolver, CLI, NAPI binding, and Vite plugin all work and are fully tested. Config file loading, cross-package `.d.ts` resolution, watch mode, plugin architecture, TOON token-optimized output format, JSON schema export, LSP server scaffold, and bounded atomic DTS caching are all fully implemented and verified.

## Numbers

- 545 Rust tests (77 cli + 443 core unit + 8 snapshot + 1 core compile-fail + 16 napi binding), 36 vitest (33 unit, mocked NAPI + 3 integration against the real native binding — `packages/vite-plugin/tests/integration/`, gated on a locally-built `.node` binary, auto-skips otherwise) — all green
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -D warnings` clean with `unsafe_code = "deny"` enforced workspace-wide
- 20 real-world fixture libraries validated against `react-docgen-typescript` (shadcn, Radix, MUI, Chakra, Mantine, React Aria, antd, ariakit, ark-ui, base-ui, blueprint, day-picker, fluentui, headlessui, panda, react-final-form, react-resizable-panels, storybook-emotion, tanstack-table, zendesk-garden — see `rdt-coverage.md`)

## Features and improvements

- **Testing Stack** — `cargo-nextest` process runner, `rstest` parameterized spec tables, `insta` snapshots, and `trycmd` executable Markdown CLI specs.
- **Plugin system** (`DocgenPlugin` / `PluginRegistry`) — Extensible AST and component resolution hooks in `crates/core/src/plugin.rs`.
- **TOON output format** (`--format toon` / `toon.rs`) — Token-optimized format for LLM agents, cutting context window token usage by ~65-75%.
- **JSON schema export** (`oxc-react-docgen schema`) — Machine-readable Draft-07 JSON Schema export for component metadata validation.
- **Atomic & Bounded DTS cache** (`cache.rs`) — Atomic temp-file swap writes, dirty flag tracking, and 5,000 entry eviction cap.
- **LSP server scaffold** (`oxc-react-docgen lsp`) — bounded framing plus initialize/shutdown/exit lifecycle. It currently advertises `hoverProvider: false` and does not serve component prop hovers yet.
- **Strict Safe Rust** — `unsafe_code = "deny"` via `[workspace.lints]`, active across all three crates (`core`, `cli`, `binding`) — none currently use `unsafe`, including the NAPI FFI boundary (napi-rs's `#[napi]` macros generate the glue without user-visible `unsafe`).

## Known gaps that won't get fixed without a type checker

See the "Known gaps summary" table in `rdt-coverage.md` for the full, maintained list. The short version: conditional types, mapped types over an unbound generic, and a couple of `@emotion/styled`-specific call shapes all need real type inference OXC deliberately doesn't do. Not bugs. An opt-in TypeScript 7 semantic backend is designed but not implemented: see ADR 0006 and `type-checker-integration.md`.

## Where to look next

- **Edge cases, failure modes, and gaps not yet fixed** → `edge-cases.md` — comprehensive audit of crash/hang risks, silent data loss, and silent correctness bugs across every subsystem, prioritized. Update it as findings get fixed or new ones turn up.
- **Why those gaps happened, and the plan to fix them** → `root-cause-analysis.md` — the edge-case findings collapsed into 11 mechanism-level root causes with concrete fix proposals, plus a Phase 1 task breakdown.
- **What broke and why, historically** → `rdt-coverage.md` — every bug found during real-library validation, root cause, and the fix. Keep this updated; it's the project's memory.
- **Why a hard-to-reverse decision was made** → `docs/adr/` — OXC over the TypeScript compiler, manual serde for `PropType`, positional msgpack encoding, panic containment, the TypeScript 7 semantic backend. Write a new one when you make a decision like these (see `docs/adr/README.md`).
- **How the pipeline fits together** → `ARCHITECTURE.md`
- **Setup, testing, code style, commit conventions** → `CONTRIBUTING.md`
- **Migrating from react-docgen-typescript** → `MIGRATING.md`
- **Old build-out specs, resolved questions, point-in-time analyses** → `docs/archive/` — historical, not current, kept for reference

# Status

**Updated:** 2026-09-28

Core extraction, resolver, CLI, NAPI binding, and Vite plugin all work and are fully tested. Config file loading, cross-package `.d.ts` resolution, watch mode, plugin architecture, TOON token-optimized output format, JSON schema export, LSP server scaffold, and bounded atomic DTS caching are all fully implemented and verified.

## Numbers

- 545 Rust tests (77 cli + 443 core unit + 8 snapshot + 1 core compile-fail + 16 napi binding), 36 vitest (33 unit, mocked NAPI + 3 integration against the real native binding — `packages/vite-plugin/tests/integration/`, gated on a locally-built `.node` binary, auto-skips otherwise) — all green
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -D warnings` clean with `unsafe_code = "deny"` enforced workspace-wide
- 20 real-world fixture libraries validated against `react-docgen-typescript` (shadcn, Radix, MUI, Chakra, Mantine, React Aria, antd, ariakit, ark-ui, base-ui, blueprint, day-picker, fluentui, headlessui, panda, react-final-form, react-resizable-panels, storybook-emotion, tanstack-table, zendesk-garden — see `rdt-coverage.md`)

## Features and improvements

- **Testing Stack** — `cargo-nextest` process runner, `rstest` parameterized spec tables, `insta` snapshots, and `trycmd` executable Markdown CLI specs.
- **Plugin system** (`DocgenPlugin` / `PluginRegistry`) — Extensible AST and component resolution hooks in `crates/core/src/plugin.rs`.
- **TOON output format** (`--format toon` / `toon.rs`) — Token-optimized format for LLM agents, cutting context window token usage by ~65-75%.
- **JSON schema export** (`oxc-react-docgen schema`) — Machine-readable Draft-07 JSON Schema export for component metadata validation.
- **Atomic & Bounded DTS cache** (`cache.rs`) — Atomic temp-file swap writes, dirty flag tracking, and 5,000 entry eviction cap.
- **LSP server scaffold** (`oxc-react-docgen lsp`) — bounded framing plus initialize/shutdown/exit lifecycle. It currently advertises `hoverProvider: false` and does not serve component prop hovers yet.
- **Strict Safe Rust** — `unsafe_code = "deny"` via `[workspace.lints]`, active across all three crates (`core`, `cli`, `binding`) — none currently use `unsafe`, including the NAPI FFI boundary (napi-rs's `#[napi]` macros generate the glue without user-visible `unsafe`).

## Known gaps that won't get fixed without a type checker

See the "Known gaps summary" table in `rdt-coverage.md` for the full, maintained list. The short version: conditional types, mapped types over an unbound generic, and a couple of `@emotion/styled`-specific call shapes all need real type inference OXC deliberately doesn't do. Not bugs.

An opt-in TypeScript 7 semantic backend is designed (ADR 0006) but not implemented. Accuracy is verified against real RDT — 0 missing/extra props on 13 hand-picked components, and re-verified against the full 44-file fixture corpus (5,508/5,522 `required` matches, 5,265/5,522 type-string matches; the gap is explained noise, not a resolver bug) — and the RDT oracle that comparison depends on now runs on its own `typescript@6` install, separate from the semantic probe's `typescript@next`. Lifecycle (crash/restart/timeout handling for the `tsc --api` process) hasn't started; see `type-checker-integration.md`'s Gates table.

## Where to look next

- **Edge cases, failure modes, and gaps not yet fixed** → `edge-cases.md` — comprehensive audit of crash/hang risks, silent data loss, and silent correctness bugs across every subsystem, prioritized. Update it as findings get fixed or new ones turn up.
- **Why those gaps happened, and the plan to fix them** → `root-cause-analysis.md` — the edge-case findings collapsed into 11 mechanism-level root causes with concrete fix proposals, plus a Phase 1 task breakdown.
- **What broke and why, historically** → `rdt-coverage.md` — every bug found during real-library validation, root cause, and the fix. Keep this updated; it's the project's memory.
- **Why a hard-to-reverse decision was made** → `docs/adr/` — OXC over the TypeScript compiler, manual serde for `PropType`, positional msgpack encoding, panic containment, the TypeScript 7 semantic backend. Write a new one when you make a decision like these (see `docs/adr/README.md`).
- **How the pipeline fits together** → `ARCHITECTURE.md`
- **Setup, testing, code style, commit conventions** → `CONTRIBUTING.md`
- **Migrating from react-docgen-typescript** → `MIGRATING.md`
- **Old build-out specs, resolved questions, point-in-time analyses** → `docs/archive/` — historical, not current, kept for reference

1	# Semantic backend (TypeScript 7)
2	
3	**Status:** designed, not implemented ([ADR 0006](adr/0006-semantic-backend-as-second-resolver.md)). `PipelineOptions::resolve_complex_types` exists and does nothing. **Last verified:** 2026-09-27. Each measurement names its nightly.
4	
5	## Next step
6	
7	Start the Rust client for the Lifecycle gate — Accuracy is re-verified and the probe is committed, so this is no longer blocked on unreproducible numbers.
8	
9	Some props can't be resolved from the AST alone. An opt-in backend asks TypeScript's checker instead, using the algorithm react-docgen-typescript (RDT) uses, and merges the answer into the structural result. Structural extraction stays the default.
10	
11	## What the structural resolver can't do
12	
13	Component prop counts from `fixtures/` with `--html-attributes full`, against RDT. Root causes are from `docs/benchmarks.md`.
14	
15	| Gap | Example | Ours | RDT |
16	| --- | --- | --: | --: |
17	| Generics through alias chains | ariakit `Props<T, O> = O & Omit<ComponentPropsWithoutRef<T>, keyof O>` | 5 | 294 |
18	| Generics through alias chains | ark-ui `SelectRoot` | 36 | 314 |
19	| Conditional types | headlessui `PropsOf<TTag>` | 14 | 246 |
20	| Mapped types over a generic | base-ui `WithBaseUIEvent<T>` | 11 | 293 |
21	| Conditional type and indexed access | fluentui `Slot<Type, ...>` | 8 | 303 |
22	| `@emotion/styled` two-argument overload | storybook-emotion `Button` | 7 | 306 |
23	
24	In the 2026-07-25 baseline, 10 of 33 compared components account for 2,696 of 2,720 missing props. The other 24 are `ref` and `key`, which this tool omits by design (`MIGRATING.md`).
25	
26	## How it works
27	
28	```
29	OXC parse → structural resolver ──────────────┐
30	                                              ├→ merge → ExtractionOutput
31	tsc --api → semantic resolver (opt-in) ───────┘
32	```
33	
34	The structural result is complete on its own and returns first. The semantic pass reads each exported component from the checker and replaces the structural props where it finds one.
35	
36	### Merge rules (proposed)
37	
38	| Field | Source |
39	| --- | --- |
40	| Props present, `type`, `required` | Semantic |
41	| `parent`, `declarations` | Semantic. `declarations` lists every declaring interface, not just the first |
42	| `description`, `tags` | Semantic JSDoc, structural if empty |
43	| `defaultValue` | Structural. RDT reads defaults from the AST too |
44	| Components tsc doesn't surface (not exported) | Structural only |
45	| Degrade diagnostics of a resolved component | Dropped |
46	
47	### What gets dropped, and where
48	
49	| Dropped | Where | Status |
50	| --- | --- | --- |
51	| `children` without a description | RDT projection only. Canonical keeps it | Done |
52	| Ambient `.d.ts` components such as `PureComponent` | Merge step | Done |
53	| `ref`, `key` | Not emitted, matching the structural path | Open |
54	| HTML and DOM attributes in curated and none mode | Semantic adapter, by declaring interface rather than by name | Open |
55	
56	### Delivery (proposed)
57	
58	The structural result returns immediately. The semantic result follows: the CLI waits for it behind an opt-in flag, and the NAPI binding exposes a second async call so the Vite plugin can patch when it resolves. Spawn `tsc` at the start of the run so it loads while extraction runs. Each result carries a content hash, and a stale one is dropped.
59	
60	## The algorithm
61	
62	Mirrors RDT 2.4.0 (`lib/parser.js`). Method names are from the 7.1 client.
63	
64	1. `getSymbolOfSourceFile(file)`, then `getExportsOfModule`.
65	2. For each export, `getTypeOfSymbol`, then `getSignaturesOfType(Call)`. A component has a signature whose first parameter is named `props` or is the only parameter. For a class, use `Construct` signatures and read `props` from the instance type.
66	3. Props type: `getTypeOfSymbolAtLocation(param, param.valueDeclaration)`. Props: the type's apparent properties, plus each member's when it is a union.
67	4. Per prop, `type` is `typeToString(getBaseConstraintOfType(t) ?? t)` with default flags, so long types truncate as they do in RDT. `required` means the symbol lacks `Optional` and has no code default.
68	5. `parent` is the first declaration's parent when that is an interface or type alias. `declarations` is every declaration's parent.
69	6. `description` and `tags` come from `getDocumentationComment` and `getJsDocTags`.
70	
71	RDT also emits any exported symbol that has a JSDoc comment but no props. We don't. In the fixture corpus, 23 of the 26 entries only RDT emits are of this kind, such as enum members, type aliases and functions.
72	
73	## TypeScript 7.1 API
74	
75	| Topic | Detail |
76	| --- | --- |
77	| Where | `microsoft/TypeScript` `main` (`7.1.0-dev`). typescript-go closed on 2026-08-20 |
78	| Timeline | Beta 2026-10-06, RC 2026-11-10, stable 2026-11-24 ([#63703](https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/issues/63703)) |
79	| Get it | `npm i typescript@next`. 7.0.x has no API |
80	| Launch | `tsc --api --async --cwd <dir>`: JSON-RPC with LSP-style `Content-Length` framing, handled concurrently. Without `--async`: msgpack over stdio, strictly serial. `--pipe` uses a socket |
81	| Stability | JS entry points are `typescript/unstable/*`. The protocol has no version handshake, so pin the build |
82	| Positions | UTF-16 code units. OXC offsets are UTF-8 bytes |
83	| Surface | 157 methods on 2026-09-19, mostly with TS 6 checker names |
84	
85	**Churn.** About 20 commits touched the protocol definition (`proto.go`) between 2026-08-20 and 2026-09-18. `updateSnapshot`, project IDs and `createProgram` params were reshaped on 09-17 and 09-18. Every call the algorithm uses ran unchanged on the 09-20 and 09-26 nightlies. Re-verify on the beta.
86	
87	**Freshness.** tsc sees an edit to a dependency only when told:
88	
89	```js
90	const s1 = await s0.update({ fileNotifications: { changed: [file] }, ensurePrograms: true })
91	```
92	
93	With the notification, the dependent component's props updated (0.5 ms update, 2.8 ms query). An unnotified disk edit stayed stale (2026-09-20).
94	
95	## Evidence
96	
97	Method: RDT 2.4.0 on typescript@6.0.3 (`apps/validate`'s RDT is pinned to a TS6 API — see "The RDT oracle" below) with the harness options (`shouldExtractLiteralValuesFromEnum`, `shouldRemoveUndefinedFromOptional`, `propFilter: { skipPropsWithoutDoc: false }`), against the algorithm above via `apps/validate/src/run-semantic.ts` on typescript@next. Run with `pnpm --filter @oxc-react-docgen/validate parity`.
98	
99	| Check | Result | Nightly |
100	| --- | --- | --- |
101	| 13 components: the 10 outliers, base-ui `MenuRoot`, shadcn `Button`, mui `Button` | 0 missing and 0 extra props. `required` 3412/3412. Type strings 3410/3412 | 09-26 |
102	| Descriptions: ariakit, MUI, fluentui, shadcn | 294/294, 311/311, 288/288, 292/292 | 09-20 |
103	| `parent`: ariakit `MenuButton` | 294/294 in 12 requests | 09-20 |
104	| Fixture corpus, 55 files in one program | 70 components in common, equal prop counts on 70/70 | 09-20 |
105	| Class components | 2/2 on a synthetic file. The corpus has none | 09-20 |
106	| Full fixture corpus, 44 files / 47 components / 5554 props, one program | 5 missing, 27 extra. `required` 5508/5522. Type strings 5265/5522. Descriptions 47/47 | 09-26 |
107	
108	Type strings match after two normalizations. tsc prints union members in internal type-id order, which differs from TS 5.9, so members are compared as a set. RDT also runs `.replace(' | undefined', '')` twice, which turns a nested `=> string | undefined` into `=> string` and loses information. Canonical output keeps it. The 2 remaining differences are nested `ref` unions in fluentui and base-ui.
109	
110	Of the corpus's 26 RDT-only entries, 23 have no props and 3 are default exports RDT names differently (mui `Button` confirmed at 311/311).
111	
112	The full-corpus run's 257 remaining mismatches, unlike the curated 13, aren't all real algorithm gaps:
113	
114	- Most are non-component exports the "single-parameter function" heuristic sweeps in — plain string-returning helpers (`antd/buttonHelpers.ts`, `headlessui/render.ts`'s `mergeProps`, `blueprint/blueprintTypes.ts`) whose "props" are `String.prototype`/`Array.prototype` members. RDT is equally permissive and picks these up too, so both tools agree these aren't components; the mismatches are TS 6 vs TS 7.1-dev lib.d.ts differences (e.g. `padStart`'s parameter renamed `maxLength`→`targetLength`) and per-run `Symbol.iterator` id suffixes, not a resolver bug.
115	- `children` without a description shows as "extra" — RDT drops it, canonical keeps it (see "What gets dropped", status Done).
116	- One real RDT bug surfaced: `rdt-compat/svg-icon.tsx` declares two `forwardRef` components (`Icon`, `Box`) in one file; RDT resolves `Box`'s `ref` and DOM-attribute types to `Icon`'s `SVGSVGElement` instead of `Box`'s own `HTMLDivElement`. The semantic algorithm gets `Box` right — RDT is the outlier.
117	
118	## Cost
119	
120	Measured through the Node client on one macOS machine, so a Rust client should be lower.
121	
122	| Measure | Result |
123	| --- | --- |
124	| Spawn and first snapshot | 33–72 ms |
125	| First checker query | 1–15 ms |
126	| Request round trip | 0.1 ms. 500 positions in one request take about 1 ms |
127	| 55-file corpus, one program | 385 ms and 937 requests. RDT in-process: 955 ms |
128	| Server memory | About 100 MB (MUI `Button`) |
129	| Structural path, for comparison | 50 ms for the whole corpus, 1.75–2.1 ms per incremental update (`docs/benchmarks.md`) |
130	
131	Trimming the process, on the MUI `Button` query (median of 5 runs, 2026-09-20). Differences under about 10 ms are noise.
132	
133	| Config                                 |   Wall |    CPU | Memory |
134	| -------------------------------------- | -----: | -----: | -----: |
135	| Default                                |  85 ms | 270 ms | 102 MB |
136	| `types: []`                            |  79 ms | 260 ms | 100 MB |
137	| `types: []`, `GOGC=off`                |  71 ms | 200 ms | 111 MB |
138	| `types: []`, `GOMAXPROCS=2`            | 114 ms | 160 ms |  99 MB |
139	| Default, plus 300 unrelated root files |  88 ms | 320 ms | 112 MB |
140	
141	Pass only the files you need as roots. The API's checker is lazy, and diagnostics and emit never run.
142	
143	## Boundaries
144	
145	- **`crates/core`** owns the semantic result type, the merge and the diagnostics. It has no I/O, no async and no protocol types. The merge lives here because `OpaqueDetail` and `ParsedProp` internals are `pub(crate)`.
146	- **Backend crate** (feature-gated, off by default) spawns `tsc --api`, speaks the protocol, and handles timeouts and supervision. `config.rs` has none of these today.
147	- **CLI and NAPI** only switch it on. Neither calls JS.
148	- **Not a `DocgenPlugin`.** The hook is synchronous and runs on the cold path only. `WatchSession::update_file` skips plugins.
149	- **Failure** leaves the structural result and adds a diagnostic. It never fails extraction.
150	- **Determinism.** Reversing the query order changed no union order across 16 props in 3 files (2026-09-20). Whether canonical output sorts unions is open (below).
151	
152	## Gates before it ships
153	
154	| Gate | Status |
155	| --- | --- |
156	| Accuracy against RDT | Passed on 13 components and re-verified on the full 47-component fixture corpus. See Evidence and not verified below |
157	| Lifecycle | Not started: missing binary, unsupported version, timeout, crash, restart storm, malformed or oversized frame, partial project failure, shutdown reaping, stale notification |
158	| Cost | Measured through the Node client. Repeat with the Rust client |
159	| Determinism | Clean and incremental runs must produce the same output |
160	| Oracle | Fixed. See below |
161	
162	## The RDT oracle
163	
164	`apps/validate` depends on `typescript@next` directly (for `run-semantic.ts`'s own `tsc --api` probe), but RDT 2.4.0 crashes on import against it (`ts.JsxEmit` is undefined). RDT now resolves its `typescript` peer to `typescript@6.0.3` instead, via the aliased `typescript-next` package dependency `run-semantic.ts` imports from — no pnpm override needed, since pnpm overrides don't reliably rewrite a peer dependency's resolution (tried `pnpm-workspace.yaml`'s `overrides: { "react-docgen-typescript>typescript": ... }`; the lockfile recorded it but RDT kept resolving against whatever `typescript` apps/validate depended on directly).
165	
166	`compare.ts`/`analyze.ts` (oxc-react-docgen vs RDT/react-docgen) still compare only name, `required`, type and default, and render our types themselves in `run-ours.ts` (objects print as `{ ... }`). Their type mismatches mix resolver and renderer differences, and description, `parent` and `declarations` are never compared. `parity.ts` (RDT vs the semantic algorithm) compares description too.
167	
168	## Open decisions
169	
170	1. **Output type.** Checker types don't fit `PropType` losslessly: `Named` has no file or symbol, `EventHandler` has no return type, `Tuple` has no optional or rest elements, and `Object` has no index signatures. Add a variant or map into existing ones. `ExtractionOutput` has no schema version, so add one first.
171	2. **`ref` and `key`.** RDT emits both, and nothing else records forwardRef metadata. Semantic mode must match whatever the structural path does.
172	3. **Trigger.** Run on every exported component or only on files with degrade diagnostics. Bare generic parameters and TypeScript utility types resolve to `Named` with no diagnostic by design, so the second misses them.
173	4. **Union order.** Sort in canonical output, or keep source order for structural results.
174	
175	## Not verified
176	
177	- A Rust client. Every measurement uses the Node client.
178	- Overloads with more than one signature, static sub-components (`Menu.Item`), and barrel re-exports, where RDT names components by the barrel file.
179	- `@default` and `@type` JSDoc overrides.
180	- Projects larger than the 44-file corpus.
181	- What the `MappedType` accessors added on 2026-09-23 ([#64397](https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/pull/64397)) expose beyond resolved properties.
182

- `children` without a description shows as "extra" — RDT drops it, canonical keeps it (see "What gets dropped", status Done).

The semantic algorithm gets `Box` right — RDT is the outlier.

## Cost

Measured through the Node client on one macOS machine, so a Rust client should be lower.

| Measure | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Spawn and first snapshot | 33–72 ms |
| First checker query | 1–15 ms |
| Request round trip | 0.1 ms. 500 positions in one request take about 1 ms |
| 55-file corpus, one program | 385 ms and 937 requests. RDT in-process: 955 ms |
| Server memory | About 100 MB (MUI `Button`) |
| Structural path, for comparison | 50 ms for the whole corpus, 1.75–2.1 ms per incremental update (`docs/benchmarks.md`) |

Trimming the process, on the MUI `Button` query (median of 5 runs, 2026-09-20). Differences under about 10 ms are noise.

| Config                                 |   Wall |    CPU | Memory |
| -------------------------------------- | -----: | -----: | -----: |
| Default                                |  85 ms | 270 ms | 102 MB |
| `types: []`                            |  79 ms | 260 ms | 100 MB |
| `types: []`, `GOGC=off`                |  71 ms | 200 ms | 111 MB |
| `types: []`, `GOMAXPROCS=2`            | 114 ms | 160 ms |  99 MB |
| Default, plus 300 unrelated root files |  88 ms | 320 ms | 112 MB |

Pass only the files you need as roots. The API's checker is lazy, and diagnostics and emit never run.

## Boundaries

- **`crates/core`** owns the semantic result type, the merge and the diagnostics. It has no I/O, no async and no protocol types. The merge lives here because `OpaqueDetail` and `ParsedProp` internals are `pub(crate)`.
- **Backend crate** (feature-gated, off by default) spawns `tsc --api`, speaks the protocol, and handles timeouts and supervision. `config.rs` has none of these today.
- **CLI and NAPI** only switch it on. Neither calls JS.
- **Not a `DocgenPlugin`.** The hook is synchronous and runs on the cold path only. `WatchSession::update_file` skips plugins.
- **Failure** leaves the structural result and adds a diagnostic. It never fails extraction.
- **Determinism.** Reversing the query order changed no union order across 16 props in 3 files (2026-09-20). Whether canonical output sorts unions is open (below).

## Gates before it ships

| Gate | Status |
| --- | --- |
| Accuracy against RDT | Passed on 13 components and re-verified on the full 47-component fixture corpus. See Evidence and not verified below |
| Lifecycle | Not started: missing binary, unsupported version, timeout, crash, restart storm, malformed or oversized frame, partial project failure, shutdown reaping, stale notification |
| Cost | Measured through the Node client. Repeat with the Rust client |
| Determinism | Clean and incremental runs must produce the same output |
| Oracle | Fixed. See below |

## The RDT oracle

`apps/validate` depends on `typescript@next` directly (for `run-semantic.ts`'s own `tsc --api` probe), but RDT 2.4.0 crashes on import against it (`ts.JsxEmit` is undefined). RDT now resolves its `typescript` peer to `typescript@6.0.3` instead, via the aliased `typescript-next` package dependency `run-semantic.ts` imports from — no pnpm override needed, since pnpm overrides don't reliably rewrite a peer dependency's resolution (tried `pnpm-workspace.yaml`'s `overrides: { "react-docgen-typescript>typescript": ... }`; the lockfile recorded it but RDT kept resolving against whatever `typescript` apps/validate depended on directly).

`compare.ts`/`analyze.ts` (oxc-react-docgen vs RDT/react-docgen) still compare only name, `required`, type and default, and render our types themselves in `run-ours.ts` (objects print as `{ ... }`). Their type mismatches mix resolver and renderer differences, and description, `parent` and `declarations` are never compared. `parity.ts` (RDT vs the semantic algorithm) compares description too.

## Open decisions

1. **Output type.** Checker types don't fit `PropType` losslessly: `Named` has no file or symbol, `EventHandler` has no return type, `Tuple` has no optional or rest elements, and `Object` has no index signatures. Add a variant or map into existing ones. `ExtractionOutput` has no schema version, so add one first.
2. **`ref` and `key`.** RDT emits both, and nothing else records forwardRef metadata. Semantic mode must match whatever the structural path does.
3. **Trigger.** Run on every exported component or only on files with degrade diagnostics. Bare generic parameters and TypeScript utility types resolve to `Named` with no diagnostic by design, so the second misses them.
4. **Union order.** Sort in canonical output, or keep source order for structural results.

## Not verified

- A Rust client. Every measurement uses the Node client.
- Overloads with more than one signature, static sub-components (`Menu.Item`), and barrel re-exports, where RDT names components by the barrel file.
- `@default` and `@type` JSDoc overrides.
- Projects larger than the 44-file corpus.
- What the `MappedType` accessors added on 2026-09-23 ([#64397](https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/pull/64397)) expose beyond resolved properties.

entries.name: EnterPlanMode
entries.description:
Use this tool proactively when you're about to start a non-trivial implementation task. Getting user sign-off on your approach before writing code prevents wasted effort and ensures alignment. This tool transitions you into plan mode where you can explore the codebase and design an implementation approach for user approval.

## When to Use This Tool

**Prefer using EnterPlanMode** for implementation tasks unless they're simple. Use it when ANY of these conditions apply:

1. **New Feature Implementation**: Adding meaningful new functionality
   - Example: "Add a logout button" - where should it go? What should happen on click?
   - Example: "Add form validation" - what rules? What error messages?

2. **Multiple Valid Approaches**: The task can be solved in several different ways
   - Example: "Add caching to the API" - could use Redis, in-memory, file-based, etc.
   - Example: "Improve performance" - many optimization strategies possible

3. **Code Modifications**: Changes that affect existing behavior or structure
   - Example: "Update the login flow" - what exactly should change?
   - Example: "Refactor this component" - what's the target architecture?

4. **Architectural Decisions**: The task requires choosing between patterns or technologies
   - Example: "Add real-time updates" - WebSockets vs SSE vs polling
   - Example: "Implement state management" - Redux vs Context vs custom solution

5. **Multi-File Changes**: The task will likely touch more than 2-3 files
   - Example: "Refactor the authentication system"
   - Example: "Add a new API endpoint with tests"

6. **Unclear Requirements**: You need to explore before understanding the full scope
   - Example: "Make the app faster" - need to profile and identify bottlenecks
   - Example: "Fix the bug in checkout" - need to investigate root cause

7. **User Preferences Matter**: The implementation could reasonably go multiple ways
   - If you would use AskUserQuestion to clarify the approach, use EnterPlanMode instead
   - Plan mode lets you explore first, then present options with context

## When NOT to Use This Tool

Only skip EnterPlanMode for simple tasks:
- Single-line or few-line fixes (typos, obvious bugs, small tweaks)
- Adding a single function with clear requirements
- Tasks where the user has given very specific, detailed instructions
- Pure research/exploration tasks (use the Agent tool instead)

## What Happens in Plan Mode

In plan mode, you'll:
1. Thoroughly explore the codebase using `find`/Glob, `grep`/Grep, and Read
2. Understand existing patterns and architecture
3. Design an implementation approach
4. Present your plan to the user for approval
5. Use AskUserQuestion if you need to clarify approaches
6. Exit plan mode with ExitPlanMode when ready to implement

## Examples

### GOOD - Use EnterPlanMode:
User: "Add user authentication to the app"
- Requires architectural decisions (session vs JWT, where to store tokens, middleware structure)

User: "Optimize the database queries"
- Multiple approaches possible, need to profile first, significant impact

User: "Implement dark mode"
- Architectural decision on theme system, affects many components

User: "Add a delete button to the user profile"
- Seems simple but involves: where to place it, confirmation dialog, API call, error handling, state updates

User: "Update the error handling in the API"
- Affects multiple files, user should approve the approach

### BAD - Don't use EnterPlanMode:
User: "Fix the typo in the README"
- Straightforward, no planning needed

User: "Add a console.log to debug this function"
- Simple, obvious implementation

User: "What files handle routing?"
- Research task, not implementation planning

## Important Notes

- This tool REQUIRES user approval - they must consent to entering plan mode
- If unsure whether to use it, err on the side of planning - it's better to get alignment upfront than to redo work
- Users appreciate being consulted before significant changes are made to their codebase

No plan file exists yet. You should create your plan at /Users/gabe/.claude/plans/mellow-purring-crystal.md using the Write tool.
You should build your plan incrementally by writing to or editing this file. NOTE that this is the only file you are allowed to edit - other than this you are only allowed to take READ-ONLY actions.

## Plan Workflow

### Phase 1: Initial Understanding
Goal: Gain a comprehensive understanding of the user's request by reading through code and asking them questions. Critical: In this phase you should only use the Explore subagent type.

1. Focus on understanding the user's request and the code associated with their request. Actively search for existing functions, utilities, and patterns that can be reused — avoid proposing new code when suitable implementations already exist.

2. **Launch up to 3 Explore agents IN PARALLEL** (single message, multiple tool calls) to efficiently explore the codebase.
   - Use 1 agent when the task is isolated to known files, the user provided specific file paths, or you're making a small targeted change.
   - Use multiple agents when: the scope is uncertain, multiple areas of the codebase are involved, or you need to understand existing patterns before planning.
   - Quality over quantity - 3 agents maximum, but you should try to use the minimum number of agents necessary (usually just 1)
   - If using multiple agents: Provide each agent with a specific search focus or area to explore. Example: One agent searches for existing implementations, another explores related components, a third investigating testing patterns

### Phase 2: Design
Goal: Design an implementation approach.

Launch Plan agent(s) to design the implementation based on the user's intent and your exploration results from Phase 1.

You can launch up to 3 agent(s) in parallel.

**Guidelines:**
- **Default**: Launch at least 1 Plan agent for most tasks - it helps validate your understanding and consider alternatives
- **Skip agents**: Only for truly trivial tasks (typo fixes, single-line changes, simple renames)
- **Multiple agents**: Use up to 3 agents for complex tasks that benefit from different perspectives

Examples of when to use multiple agents:
- The task touches multiple parts of the codebase
- It's a large refactor or architectural change
- There are many edge cases to consider
- You'd benefit from exploring different approaches

Example perspectives by task type:
- New feature: simplicity vs performance vs maintainability
- Bug fix: root cause vs workaround vs prevention
- Refactoring: minimal change vs clean architecture

In the agent prompt:
- Provide comprehensive background context from Phase 1 exploration including filenames and code path traces
- Describe requirements and constraints
- Request a detailed implementation plan

### Phase 3: Review
Goal: Review the plan(s) from Phase 2 and ensure alignment with the user's intentions.
1. Read the critical files you identified during exploration to deepen your understanding
2. Ensure that the plans align with the user's original request
3. Use AskUserQuestion to clarify any remaining questions with the user

### Phase 4: Final Plan
Goal: Write your final plan to the plan file (the only file you can edit).
- Begin with a **Context** section: explain why this change is being made — the problem or need it addresses, what prompted it, and the intended outcome
- Include only your recommended approach, not all alternatives
- Ensure that the plan file is concise enough to scan quickly, but detailed enough to execute effectively
- Name the critical files to be modified. For changes that repeat a pattern across many files, describe the pattern once and list a few representative paths — do not enumerate every file or line number
- Reference existing functions and utilities you found that should be reused, with their file paths
- Include a verification section describing how to test the changes end-to-end (run the code, use MCP tools, run tests)

### Phase 5: Call ExitPlanMode
At the very end of your turn, once you have asked the user questions and are happy with your final plan file - you should always call ExitPlanMode to indicate to the user that you are done planning.
This is critical - your turn should only end with either using the AskUserQuestion tool OR calling ExitPlanMode. Do not stop unless it's for these 2 reasons

**Important:** Use AskUserQuestion ONLY to clarify requirements or choose between approaches. Use ExitPlanMode to request plan approval. Do NOT ask about plan approval in any other way - no text questions, no AskUserQuestion. Phrases like "Is this plan okay?", "Should I proceed?", "How does this plan look?", "Any changes before we start?", or similar MUST use ExitPlanMode.

NOTE: At any point in time through this workflow you should feel free to ask the user questions or clarifications using the AskUserQuestion tool. Don't make large assumptions about user intent. The goal is to present a well researched plan to the user, and tie any loose ends before implementation begins.

input.description: Explore crate scaffolding and process-spawn patterns
input.prompt:
In this Rust/TypeScript repo (oxc-react-docgen), I'm planning a new feature-gated Rust crate that will spawn `tsc --api --async` as a child process and speak JSON-RPC with Content-Length framing over its stdin/stdout, with production-grade process lifecycle handling (crash detection, restarts, timeouts, version checks, clean shutdown).

Research and report back on:

1. **Crate scaffolding conventions.** Look at crates/core/Cargo.toml, crates/cli/Cargo.toml, crates/binding/Cargo.toml, and the workspace root Cargo.toml. What's the naming convention for new crates (package name vs directory name)? How are workspace dependencies declared/inherited (`.workspace = true` pattern)? What lints/edition/license does workspace.package set? Is there a feature-flag convention anywhere in the workspace already (grep for `[features]` across all Cargo.toml files)?

2. **Existing process-spawning code.** Read crates/cli/src/config.rs in full — it spawns node/tsx to evaluate docgen.config.ts per crates/cli/AGENTS.md's mention of "Config loading (config.rs) runs the user's docgen.config.ts via node+tsx." How does it spawn the process, handle stdout/stderr, handle spawn failure (missing binary), and handle timeouts if any? What crate does it use (std::process::Command, tokio::process::Command)?

3. **Existing Content-Length JSON-RPC framing code.** Read crates/cli/src/commands/lsp.rs in full (this is the LSP *server* — we need a *client*, but the framing logic is symmetric). Note especially: `check_content_length`, `read_content_length`, `send_response`, the `MAX_LSP_MESSAGE_*` size cap constant, and its existing tests (oversized frame, malformed/headerless frame, missing Content-Length). Report exact function signatures and the size-cap constant's value and location.

4. **Existing subprocess integration tests.** Read crates/cli/tests/lsp_process.rs in full — how does it spawn the CLI binary as a subprocess and interact with it over stdio in tests? Report the test harness pattern used (any helper crate, `assert_cmd`, raw `std::process::Command`, etc.) since a "spawn tsc --api, feed it a request, assert the response" test suite for the new crate would likely want the same harness style.

5. **Panic containment pattern.** Read crates/core/src/panic_guard.rs in full — the `contain_panic` function ADR 0005 introduced. Report its exact signature and how existing callers use it, since docs/type-checker-integration.md says the semantic backend crate should route through the same discipline where relevant.

6. **tokio usage patterns.** Grep the whole crates/ tree for `tokio::process`, `tokio::time::timeout`, `tokio::select`, `spawn_blocking` to see if there's already any async process-supervision code to model from (e.g. in crates/cli/src/commands/watch.rs, since it's long-running and needs file-change notification plumbing).

Report file paths, exact signatures/constants, and short code excerpts (not full files) for each of the 6 items above. Keep the report under 600 words plus code excerpts.

You're designing a new Rust crate for oxc-react-docgen (repo at /Users/gabe/Projects/oxc-react-codegen). Do NOT write any files — this is a planning task only. Produce a detailed, concrete implementation plan as your final answer.

## Goal

ADR 0006 (docs/adr/0006-semantic-backend-as-second-resolver.md) and docs/type-checker-integration.md describe an opt-in semantic backend that spawns TypeScript 7.1's `tsc --api --async --cwd <dir>` and speaks JSON-RPC over its stdio (Content-Length framing, like LSP) to ask the real TypeScript checker questions a structural (AST-only) resolver can't answer. The doc's "Gates before it ships" table lists a Lifecycle gate that's "Not started": **missing binary, unsupported version, timeout, crash, restart storm, malformed or oversized frame, partial project failure, shutdown reaping, stale notification**.

Scope for THIS task (confirmed with the user): build ONLY the new feature-gated crate — the process supervisor + JSON-RPC transport client that satisfies the Lifecycle gate. Do NOT touch crates/core's types, add a CLI flag, or add a NAPI option — those depend on still-open decisions (how checker types map to `PropType`, ref/key handling) that are explicitly out of scope. This crate should be usable/testable standalone, with no consumer wiring it up yet.

## Research already done (don't re-explore, use this)

**Workspace conventions** (root Cargo.toml, crates/*/Cargo.toml):
- `[workspace.package]`: edition 2021, rust-version 1.94, license AGPL-3.0-or-later.
- `[workspace.lints.rust] unsafe_code = "deny"`; `[workspace.lints.clippy] all = { level = "warn", priority = -1 }`.
- `tokio = { version = "1.52", features = ["rt-multi-thread", "process", "io-util", "sync", "macros"] }` already in `[workspace.dependencies]` — process spawning and async I/O are available, but currently UNUSED anywhere in crates/ (only `tokio::task::spawn_blocking` appears, in crates/binding/src/lib.rs, wrapping sync core calls for NAPI's async boundary). No `tokio::process`, `tokio::time::timeout`, or `tokio::select` exists yet anywhere — this crate would be the first real async I/O code in the workspace.
- Package naming: directory `crates/core`/`crates/cli`/`crates/binding`, package name `oxc-react-docgen-core`/`oxc-react-docgen`/`oxc-react-docgen-napi`. A new crate at `crates/<dir>` should be named `oxc-react-docgen-<dir>`.
- Member Cargo.tomls use `version.workspace = true`, `edition.workspace = true`, `license.workspace = true`, `[lints] workspace = true`, deps as `depname.workspace = true` where shared.
- **No `[features]` table exists anywhere in the workspace yet** — this crate/its consumer will be the first precedent for feature-gating. Since nothing consumes it yet in this pass, the crate itself can just always compile; gating happens later when something imports it.

- `fn check_content_length(len: usize) -> Result<()>` — rejects over-cap.
- `fn read_content_length<R: BufRead>(reader: &mut R) -> Result<Option<usize>, ()>` — reads header lines until blank line; `Err(())` means true EOF before any header; `Ok(None)` means a header block was read but had no usable `Content-Length:` line (must hard-error, not silently continue, or the stream desyncs).
- `fn send_response<W: Write>(out: &mut W, response: &serde_json::Value)` — writes `Content-Length: {len}\r\n\r\n{body}`.
- Existing tests cover: oversized frame rejected, exactly-at-cap accepted, headerless/malformed frame reported distinctly from EOF, unparsable Content-Length value, true EOF vs mid-header disconnect, non-UTF8 header bytes, broken-pipe write failure (logged, not panicked).
- This is all SYNC std::io (`BufRead`/`Write`), server role (reads requests, writes responses). The new crate needs an ASYNC CLIENT-role equivalent (reads responses/notifications, writes requests) using `tokio::io::AsyncBufRead`/`AsyncWrite` — same parsing logic and same test scenarios should be mirrored, not copied verbatim.

**Existing process-spawn precedent** (crates/cli/src/config.rs's `try_load_config`, spawns node+tsx to eval docgen.config.ts): uses `std::process::Command` (sync, not tokio), piped stdio, `child.wait_with_output()`, spawn failure wrapped with a clear "is node installed and on PATH?" message, NO timeout logic at all, config path passed via env var not a shell string (injection safety — mentioned in crates/cli/AGENTS.md as a real rule: "Config loading (config.rs) runs the user's docgen.config.ts via node+tsx. This crate should apply the same care for any user/environment-controlled string it passes to the child process (the `--cwd` argument, the resolved `tsc` binary path).

- Launch: `tsc --api --async --cwd <dir>` → JSON-RPC with LSP-style Content-Length framing over stdio, "handled concurrently" (i.e. multiple in-flight requests, responses can arrive out of order, must be correlated by request id — standard JSON-RPC 2.0 shape presumably, though the doc doesn't show a raw wire example, just describes behavior at the `typescript/unstable/async` JS client layer wrapping it).

- Freshness: a dependent file only gets picked up when explicitly told, via an `updateSnapshot`-shaped call carrying `fileNotifications: { changed: [file] }`. A notification that arrives late/out of order relative to a query is the "stale notification" lifecycle concern — the client needs to track "last update actually applied" vs "update requested" so a caller can't be told stale data was fresh.
- Cost data (Node client, for comparison only): spawn+first snapshot 33-72ms, first checker query 1-15ms, request round trip ~0.1ms, 55-file corpus 385ms/937 requests, server memory ~100MB.

1. **Crate location, name, Cargo.toml** — directory, package name, dependencies (tokio subset needed, serde/serde_json, thiserror or similar for the error type, any others), dev-dependencies for the fake-tsc test binary.
2. **Module layout** — e.g. transport (framing), client (request/response + notifications, request-id correlation), supervisor (spawn/version-check/timeout/restart/shutdown), error types. Give a concrete file tree.
3. **The async Content-Length framing reader/writer** — concrete function signatures (async, generic over `tokio::io::AsyncRead`/`AsyncWrite` or concrete over the child's piped stdio), reusing the size-cap-before-allocating and malformed-vs-EOF distinction from lsp.rs's tested design.
4. **Request/response correlation** — how concurrent in-flight requests get matched to responses (a request-id counter + a map of pending oneshot channels is the standard tokio pattern — confirm or propose alternative), and how server-initiated notifications (if any) are handled separately from responses.
5. **Process supervisor design, one paragraph or bullet list per Lifecycle-gate item:**
   - missing binary (spawn fails)
   - unsupported version (pinned version check before/at startup)
   - timeout (per-request deadline via `tokio::time::timeout`)
   - crash (child exits unexpectedly mid-session — how is this detected: watching the child's exit future, or a failed write/read?)
   - restart storm (bounded retry with backoff — propose exact numbers, e.g. max N restarts per time window, then give up and surface a permanent error)
   - malformed or oversized frame (reuse the lsp.rs-style cap+distinct-error-kind approach)
   - partial project failure (some files in a multi-file `createProgram` call fail to resolve — how does the client surface partial success vs total failure to its caller?)
   - shutdown reaping (explicit `close()`/`Drop` behavior: send a shutdown request if the protocol has one, else just kill; always `.wait()` the child so it's not left as a zombie, with a bounded grace period before force-kill)
   - stale notification (how the client tracks freshness so a caller can't be handed data from before a notification was applied)
6. **The error type** — a single crate-level error enum covering all of the above distinctly enough that a caller (or a test) can assert on which failure mode occurred.
7. **Public API sketch** — the handful of types/functions a future consumer (crates/core's merge step, eventually) would call: how you spawn/connect, how you send a raw JSON-RPC request generically (since the actual checker methods aren't being implemented in this pass), how you shut down.
8. **Fake-tsc test harness** — propose a small Rust `[[bin]]` test-helper binary (not a shell script — this workspace builds on Windows CI, confirmed via cargo-deny's windows-target entries in Cargo.lock) that can be told via env var or args which Lifecycle scenario to simulate (never start responding / wrong version string / hang forever / exit code N after M requests / emit garbage bytes / emit an oversized Content-Length / etc.), and sketch the test file(s) that would exercise each of the 9 Lifecycle-gate items against it, one test per item minimum.
9. **What's explicitly NOT built in this pass** — restate: no crates/core wiring, no CLI/NAPI flags, no actual checker-method calls (getSymbolOfSourceFile etc.) beyond whatever minimal request the tests need to prove lifecycle behavior (e.g. an `initialize` call and maybe a trivial `parseConfigFile`/`createProgram` round trip if needed to test partial-project-failure and stale-notification realistically) — note where the algorithm implementation would plug in later without redesigning the transport/supervisor.

Give me a concrete, opinionated plan — not a menu of options. Pick a design for each numbered item above and justify it briefly against the research facts given. Keep the whole thing readable — use headers and code-signature sketches, not prose walls.

```rust
pub const DEFAULT_MAX_FRAME_BYTES: usize = 16 * 1024 * 1024; // matches crates/cli lsp.rs's cap

pub fn check_frame_len(len: usize, cap: usize) -> Result<(), TscClientError>;

/// any header; `Ok(None)` = header block read but no usable Content-Length
/// (caller must treat as fatal — stream is desynced, not just "no length").
pub async fn read_content_length<R>(reader: &mut R) -> Result<Option<usize>, FramingEof>
where R: tokio::io::AsyncBufRead + Unpin;

/// Full frame read: EOF-before-header -> Ok(None); malformed header -> Err(MalformedFrame);
/// oversized -> Err(OversizedFrame) *before* allocating; EOF mid-body -> Err(MalformedFrame(TruncatedBody)).
pub async fn read_frame<R>(reader: &mut R, cap: usize) -> Result<Option<Vec<u8>>, TscClientError>
where R: tokio::io::AsyncBufRead + Unpin;

pub async fn write_frame<W>(writer: &mut W, body: &[u8]) -> std::io::Result<()>
```

Standard tokio pattern, `dashmap` (already a workspace dep) over a single `Mutex<HashMap>` for the pending-request table:

```rust
#[derive(Clone)]
pub struct Client(Arc<ClientInner>);

struct ClientInner {
    stdin: tokio::sync::Mutex<tokio::process::ChildStdin>,   // serializes concurrent writers
    pending: DashMap<u64, oneshot::Sender<Result<TaggedResponse, TscClientError>>>,
    next_id: AtomicU64,
    next_seq: AtomicU64,                                      // wire-arrival order stamp, see §5 stale notification
    notifications: Mutex<Option<mpsc::UnboundedReceiver<Notification>>>, // taken exactly once
    child_exited: watch::Receiver<Option<std::process::ExitStatus>>,
    shutdown_requested: AtomicBool,
}
```

One background reader task (spawned at connect) owns `ChildStdout`, loops `transport::read_frame`, and dispatches by shape: has `"id"` and (`"result"` or `"error"`) → pop `pending`, complete the oneshot; has `"method"` and no `"id"` → push onto the notifications `mpsc`; unparsable body → log + drop (recoverable, see §5). ## 4. Request/response correlation

```rust

struct ClientInner {
    stdin: tokio::sync::Mutex<tokio::process::ChildStdin>,   // serializes concurrent writers
    pending: DashMap<u64, oneshot::Sender<Result<TaggedResponse, TscClientError>>>,
    next_id: AtomicU64,
```

# Rust `tsc --api` client — satisfy the Lifecycle gate

## Context

ADR 0006 (`docs/adr/0006-semantic-backend-as-second-resolver.md`) accepted an opt-in semantic backend: spawn TypeScript 7.1's `tsc --api --async` and ask the real checker questions the structural (AST-only) resolver can't answer (conditional types, mapped types over a generic, etc. — see `docs/type-checker-integration.md`, "What the structural resolver can't do"). Shipping it needs four gates green: Accuracy, Oracle, Cost, Lifecycle (`docs/type-checker-integration.md`, "Gates before it ships"). This session already closed Accuracy (re-verified against the full 44-file fixture corpus) and Oracle (fixed RDT's TypeScript 7 incompatibility). Lifecycle — "missing binary, unsupported version, timeout, crash, restart storm, malformed or oversized frame, partial project failure, shutdown reaping, stale notification" — is listed "Not started," and the doc's own "Next step" now points here.

**Scope for this pass (confirmed with the user):** build only the process-supervisor + JSON-RPC transport crate that satisfies Lifecycle, standalone and tested against a fake `tsc`. No `crates/core` wiring, no CLI flag, no NAPI option, no real `typescript/unstable/*` checker methods — those depend on the still-open "Output type" and `ref`/`key` decisions in `type-checker-integration.md`'s "Open decisions," which are a separate follow-up once this lands.

## Approach

New workspace member `crates/tsc-client` (package `oxc-react-docgen-tsc-client`), added to root `Cargo.toml`'s `members`. No `[features]` table yet — nothing consumes it in this pass, so it just compiles as an ordinary crate; feature-gating happens when a consumer wires it in later.

Reuses two proven patterns already in this repo instead of inventing new ones:
- **Content-Length framing** — `crates/cli/src/commands/lsp.rs`'s tested design (16 MiB cap checked *before* allocating, EOF-before-header vs. no-usable-header-line treated as distinct outcomes) ported from sync std::io/server-role to async `tokio::io`/client-role. Same test scenarios, mirrored not copied.
- **Injection-safe process spawning** — `crates/cli/src/config.rs`'s node/tsx spawn (env var for paths, not shell strings; clear "is X installed?" hint on spawn failure) is the model for spawning `tsc`.

### Module layout

```
crates/tsc-client/
  Cargo.toml
  src/
    lib.rs              — public API re-exports
    error.rs             — TscClientError (thiserror), MalformedFrameReason
    protocol.rs           — JSON-RPC envelope types, RequestId
    transport/
      mod.rs
      framing.rs           — async Content-Length reader/writer (also used by fake-tsc, so client and
                              fake server can't drift on wire format)
    client.rs             — Client: request/response correlation, notifications, freshness (seq) tracking
    supervisor.rs           — Supervisor: version check, spawn, crash detection, restart policy, shutdown/reap
  tests/
    bin/fake_tsc.rs         — scenario-driven fake tsc process, a real [[bin]] (not a shell script — this
                              workspace builds on Windows CI), scenario selected via FAKE_TSC_SCENARIO env var
    common/mod.rs           — spawn_fake(scenario) test helper
    lifecycle_missing_binary.rs
    lifecycle_unsupported_version.rs
    lifecycle_timeout.rs
    lifecycle_crash.rs
    lifecycle_restart_storm.rs
    lifecycle_malformed_or_oversized_frame.rs
    lifecycle_partial_project_failure.rs
    lifecycle_shutdown_reaping.rs
    lifecycle_stale_notification.rs
```

`transport/` as a `mod.rs`-directory matches `crates/core`'s existing `extractor/`, `resolver/`, `types/`, `pipeline/` convention.

### Cargo.toml

All of `tokio` (add `"time"` feature to the existing workspace set for `timeout`/`test-util`), `serde`, `serde_json`, `camino`, `tracing`, `dashmap`, `tempfile` are **already workspace dependencies** (verified against root `Cargo.toml` and `crates/core`/`crates/cli`/`crates/binding`) — declare with `.workspace = true`. `thiserror = "2"` is the one new dependency, declared as a plain crate-local version string (not added to `[workspace.dependencies]`) — this repo already has that exact precedent for single-consumer deps (`crates/cli/Cargo.toml`'s `comfy-table = "7.0"`, `crossterm = "0.28"`). `miette` (the workspace's CLI-facing diagnostic renderer) isn't appropriate here — this is a library error type, not user-facing terminal output, and `crates/core` itself uses a plain custom type rather than miette for the same reason.

```toml
[[bin]]
name = "fake-tsc"
path = "tests/bin/fake_tsc.rs"

[dependencies]
tokio      = { workspace = true, features = ["time"] }
serde.workspace      = true
serde_json.workspace = true
camino.workspace     = true
tracing.workspace    = true
dashmap.workspace    = true
thiserror  = "2"

[dev-dependencies]
tokio      = { workspace = true, features = ["time", "test-util"] }
tempfile.workspace = true
```

**Why no `panic_guard`-style containment here:** `crates/core::panic_guard::contain_panic` exists to contain panics from caller-supplied closures on rayon/NAPI boundaries. This crate never runs an arbitrary caller closure — its only untrusted input is bytes from a child process, handled through `Result`, never `.unwrap()`/`.expect()`. State that as a deliberate decision in the crate's module doc.

### Transport: async Content-Length framing (`transport/framing.rs`)

```rust
pub const DEFAULT_MAX_FRAME_BYTES: usize = 16 * 1024 * 1024; // matches lsp.rs's cap

pub async fn read_frame<R>(reader: &mut R, cap: usize) -> Result<Option<Vec<u8>>, TscClientError>
where R: tokio::io::AsyncBufRead + Unpin;
// EOF before any header -> Ok(None). Header block read but no usable Content-Length,
// or truncated body -> Err(MalformedFrame) (fatal — stream position is no longer known).
// Declared length over cap -> Err(OversizedFrame), checked BEFORE allocating the buffer.

pub async fn write_frame<W>(writer: &mut W, body: &[u8]) -> std::io::Result<()>
where W: tokio::io::AsyncWrite + Unpin;
```

Mirror `lsp.rs`'s existing unit tests (oversized rejected, exactly-at-cap accepted, headerless vs. true EOF distinguished, unparsable Content-Length, truncated body) as async equivalents directly in `framing.rs`, before any integration-level test exercises the same behavior through a real child process.

### Client: request/response correlation (`client.rs`)

```rust
#[derive(Clone)]
pub struct Client(Arc<ClientInner>);

struct ClientInner {
    stdin: tokio::sync::Mutex<tokio::process::ChildStdin>,
    pending: DashMap<u64, tokio::sync::oneshot::Sender<Result<TaggedResponse, TscClientError>>>,
    next_id: AtomicU64,
    next_seq: AtomicU64,                                    // wire-arrival order, for stale-notification checks
    notifications: tokio::sync::Mutex<Option<tokio::sync::mpsc::UnboundedReceiver<Notification>>>,
}

pub struct TaggedResponse { pub value: serde_json::Value, pub seq: u64 }

impl Client {
    pub async fn request(&self, method: &str, params: serde_json::Value, deadline: std::time::Duration)
        -> Result<TaggedResponse, TscClientError>;
    pub fn take_notifications(&self) -> Option<tokio::sync::mpsc::UnboundedReceiver<Notification>>;
}
```

One background task (spawned at connect) owns `ChildStdout`, loops `read_frame`, and dispatches by shape: has `id` + (`result`|`error`) → complete the matching `pending` oneshot; has `method`, no `id` → push to the notifications channel; unparsable body → log and drop (recoverable — a malformed *body* doesn't desync the stream, only a malformed *header* does). A single `fail_all_pending(err)` path (called on crash or fatal framing error) drains `pending` and closes the notifications channel.

### Supervisor: one decision per Lifecycle item (`supervisor.rs`)

- **Missing binary** — `tokio::process::Command::new(tsc_path).spawn()` failing → `SpawnFailed { path, source }` with a config.rs-style "install `typescript@next` or pass an explicit path" hint. No retry.
- **Unsupported version** — read `tsc_path`'s adjacent `package.json` `"version"` field *before spawning* (no protocol round trip, no process cost for a doomed launch) and compare against a compiled-in pinned allowlist. Mismatch → `UnsupportedVersion`; unreadable/unparsable → `VersionCheckFailed`.
- **Timeout** — `request()` takes an explicit `deadline: Duration` (no crate-wide default; Cost table shows call cost ranges from ~1ms to ~400ms) and wraps the oneshot await in `tokio::time::timeout`. Only the internal handshake gets a built-in constant (`DEFAULT_HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT = 10s` against a measured 33–72ms). On elapse: remove the pending entry (a late response becomes a no-op send) and return `Timeout { method, after }`.
- **Crash** — two signals converge on one `fail_all_pending`: a dedicated task awaits `child.wait()` once; the reader task's own loop hits EOF/IO error. Whichever fires first wins; the other is a no-op (oneshots already completed).
- **Restart storm** — bounded: `MAX_RESTARTS = 3` within `RESTART_WINDOW = 60s`, backoff `200ms → 400ms → 800ms` (capped `5s`). Exceeding the cap moves the `Supervisor` to a terminal failed state; every later call short-circuits with `RestartStormDetected` without touching the process again.
- **Malformed/oversized frame** — malformed **header** is fatal (byte offset of the next frame is unrecoverable) and routes through `fail_all_pending`; malformed **JSON body** (Content-Length was valid) is recoverable — log and drop that one frame. Oversized is fatal, checked pre-allocation, cap configurable (`SupervisorConfig::max_frame_bytes`, default `DEFAULT_MAX_FRAME_BYTES`) so tests don't need to push 16 MiB over a pipe.
- **Partial project failure** — no batching/aggregation in this crate: `request()` is per-call. A well-formed JSON-RPC `error` response scopes to that one request (`RpcError { code, message, data }`) and never touches a concurrently in-flight sibling — that per-call/session-wide error distinction (`RpcError` vs. `Crashed`/`RestartStormDetected`) is what a future merge step needs to tell "this component failed" from "the whole run failed."
- **Shutdown reaping** — `pub async fn shutdown(self) -> Result<(), TscClientError>`: mark shutting-down first (so the crash-watcher doesn't misreport a clean exit), drop `ChildStdin` (EOF), race a 2s grace `child.wait()`, `kill()` on timeout, then **unconditionally** `wait()` again so the child is always reaped. `Drop` is a non-blocking best-effort `start_kill()` + `tracing::warn!` fallback only — the real guarantee lives in `.shutdown()`.
- **Stale notification** — `next_seq` stamps every inbound frame in true wire-arrival order (not issue order, not wall clock); `TaggedResponse.seq` lets a caller mechanically check "could this answer reflect an update I already got acked?" (`answer.seq > update_ack.seq`) without needing the real (still-churning) `updateSnapshot` wire shape.

**One refinement on top of this design:** a bare `Client` handle is tied to one child process's `ClientInner` — after a Supervisor-driven restart, old `Client` clones held by a caller are permanently `SessionClosed`. Give `Supervisor` its own `pub async fn request(...)` that fetches the current `Client`, and on `Crashed` (with restart budget remaining) restarts once and retries the same call once before propagating; `Supervisor::client()` stays available for a caller that wants the low-level handle without that retry behavior.

```rust
pub struct SupervisorConfig {
    pub tsc_path: camino::Utf8PathBuf,
    pub cwd: camino::Utf8PathBuf,
    pub handshake_timeout: std::time::Duration,  // default 10s
    pub max_frame_bytes: usize,                  // default DEFAULT_MAX_FRAME_BYTES
}

impl Supervisor {
    pub async fn spawn(config: SupervisorConfig) -> Result<Self, TscClientError>;
    pub fn client(&self) -> Client;
    pub async fn request(&self, method: &str, params: serde_json::Value, deadline: std::time::Duration)
        -> Result<TaggedResponse, TscClientError>;   // restart-on-crash, retried once
    pub async fn shutdown(self) -> Result<(), TscClientError>;
}
```

### Error type (`error.rs`)

One `thiserror`-derived enum, one variant family per Lifecycle item so a test can assert on which failure mode fired: `SpawnFailed`, `UnsupportedVersion`, `VersionCheckFailed`, `Timeout`, `Crashed`, `RestartStormDetected`, `OversizedFrame`, `MalformedFrame(MalformedFrameReason)`, `RpcError`, `SessionClosed`, `Write`.

### Fake-tsc test harness (`tests/bin/fake_tsc.rs`)

A real tokio `[[bin]]`, not a shell script (this workspace builds on Windows CI — confirmed via `Cargo.lock`'s Windows target entries). Scenario picked via `FAKE_TSC_SCENARIO` env var (env-over-argv, matching `config.rs`'s precedent for test/caller-controlled input): `never_respond`, `hang_after_n:<N>`, `exit_after:<N>:<code>`, `garbage_bytes`, `bad_content_length`, `oversized_frame:<N>`, `truncated_body`, `echo` (baseline; honors `params.fail` to emit an `error` object), `reorder_ack` (answers request 2 before request 1), `shutdown_slow:<ms>`.

Built against this crate's own `transport::{read_frame, write_frame}` for every "valid frame" scenario so the fake server can't drift from what the real client parses; "bad frame" scenarios intentionally hand-write raw bytes instead.

One test file per Lifecycle item, each spawning `env!("CARGO_BIN_EXE_fake-tsc")` through a shared `tests/common/mod.rs` helper and asserting on the specific `TscClientError` variant (or, for shutdown reaping: wall-clock bound + process no longer alive; for stale notification: `seq` ordering).

### Explicitly not built this pass

No resolution of `node_modules/typescript/bin/tsc` — `tsc_path` is caller-supplied. A future consumer plugs in via `Supervisor::request("typescript/unstable/...", json!({...}), deadline)` with no transport/supervisor redesign needed.

## Verification

- `cargo test -p oxc-react-docgen-tsc-client` — unit tests in `framing.rs` (mirrored from `lsp.rs`'s cases) plus one integration test per Lifecycle item (9 files) against `fake-tsc`, all green.
